headline: Highest risk is medium: shared-memory orchestration can pass unverified outputs between Semantic Kernel and Superset, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Semantic Kernel can use MCP servers and shared memory-store state, while Superset exposes an API and can consume application-defined files. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from one side can influence the other in default orchestration patterns. The pair is not provably isolated, so uncertainty stays at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Semantic Kernel forwards MCP or memory-store content into prompts consumed by Superset workflows
IF Superset ingests API/file content from the shared workspace without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of shared-memory content into prompts
Add provenance tags to all cross-agent messages
Restrict Superset API inputs to allowlisted schemas

B_data_leakage.rationale: Semantic Kernel explicitly handles model-provider API keys and plugin credentials and has broad network egress; Superset is a data-engineering system with API access. If they share a workspace or memory store, sensitive application context can flow from A into B outputs or outbound requests. The profiles do not prove isolation, so the safer medium rating applies.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or memory store
IF Semantic Kernel places secrets or application context into prompts or files that Superset can read

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Semantic Kernel can write the filesystem and use MCP; Superset can call its API and has allowlisted egress. Even without explicit git overlap, both can mutate shared resources if orchestrated against the same workspace or backend. Because locking is not documented, concurrent writes remain a realistic default risk.
conditions: IF both agents target the same writable directory or shared backend
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking or optimistic concurrency

D_cascading_error.rationale: Semantic Kernel is a general agent framework that can emit tool outputs, and Superset can act on API-driven analytics workflows. If Superset treats Semantic Kernel output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect dashboards or actions. The pair lacks documented verification boundaries, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF Superset consumes Semantic Kernel output without validation
IF downstream workflows use that output to generate reports or trigger actions
mitigations: Require human review for cross-agent outputs
Log source attribution on every handoff

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, but Semantic Kernel explicitly handles secrets and broad egress while Superset has allowlisted egress and no declared data-class handling. The main compliance issue is policy mismatch if regulated data is routed through the pair; the profiles do not show a default residency breach, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through Semantic Kernel plugins or Superset datasets
IF retention or residency policies differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Block regulated data from shared flows
